title_en: Best of Habit Formation: Katy Milkman
title_zh: Best of 习惯养成：Katy Milkman
subtitle_zh: Katy Milkman 谈习惯改变：新起点、拖延、从众，如何让改变真正持久。
description: Best of Habit Formation: Katy Milkman

turns.en: I'm Ted Sides, and this is Capital Allocators. For the second year, our summer series will share some of the best episodes of the past, curated from our favorites and yours.
turns.zh: 我是 Ted Seides，这里是 Capital Allocators。夏季系列（Summer Series）进入第二年，我们会分享一些过去最精彩的节目——从我们和你们的最爱里挑出来。

turns.en: You can pull down many of the great ones on our Spotify playlists. This series pushes them to your regular listening feed. Our 2026 summer series focuses on improving the investment process.
turns.zh: 很多精彩的节目都可以在我们的 Spotify 播放列表里听到。这个系列会把它们推送到你日常收听的信息流里。我们 2026 年的夏季系列聚焦于'改进投资流程'。

turns.en: Over the next six weeks, we'll share 10 gems from interdisciplinary skill sets that will help you level up your investing across decision-making, interviewing, storytelling, negotiations, and habit formation.
turns.zh: 接下来六周，我们会分享 10 期跨学科的宝藏节目，帮你在决策、访谈、讲故事、谈判、习惯养成（habit formation）上把投资水平再抬一档。

turns.en: This week's summer series concludes with a twofer on habits. There may be no better way to improve the investment process than to understand what it takes to improve ourselves.
turns.zh: 本周夏季系列以'习惯'的双拼（twofer）收尾。要说改进投资流程，也许没有比'理解如何提升自己'更好的路径。

turns.en: And we've got two of the best, James Clear and Katie Milkman, experts and authors of the wildly bestselling books, Atomic Habits, and How to Change.
turns.zh: 我们请到两位最棒的专家——James Clear 和 Katy Milkman——他们分别是超级畅销书《Atomic Habits》和《How to Change》的作者。

turns.en: Before we get to the interview, we're excited to introduce the next chapter of Capital Allocators University, an online on-demand curriculum with an annual in-person gathering for investment professionals committed to continuous learning.
turns.zh: 进入访谈之前，我们想先介绍 Capital Allocators University 的下一章——一套在线按需课程（on-demand curriculum），加上面向投资专业人士的年度线下聚会，专为持续学习者准备。

turns.en: One of the great ironies of investing is that the skills that matter most over a long career are often the ones least formally taught. Things like decision-making, communication, leadership, time management, interviewing, and building relationships.
turns.zh: 投资里一个大讽刺是：在整个职业生涯里最重要的那些技能，往往恰恰是最少被系统教过的——比如决策、沟通、领导力、时间管理、访谈、建立关系。

turns.en: That's why we've evolved Capital Allocators University into an online on-demand experience, making those lessons accessible to investment professionals everywhere.
turns.zh: 所以我们把 Capital Allocators University 升级成了一门在线按需课程，让各地的投资专业人士都能方便地学到这些内容。

turns.en: The best careers don't compound through knowledge alone. They compound through knowledge and relationships. If you'd like to explore the curriculum or someone on your team comes to mind, visit the link in our show notes or the university page on our website.
turns.zh: 最好的职业生涯不是只靠知识在复利，而是靠知识和人脉一起复利。如果你想了解这套课程，或者想到了团队里的某个人，请访问节目说明里的链接，或者我们官网上的 University 页面。

turns.en: Katie, thanks so much for joining me. Thanks so much for having me. I'd love to just start with how someone goes about on a path to academic research and studying change.
turns.zh: Katy，特别高兴你来做客。——谢谢邀请。——我想先聊：一个人是怎么走上'做学术研究、研究改变'这条路的。

turns.en: Well, my road was very winding, so I'm not sure I'm the example of how one goes about this, but I went about it as an engineer, actually. As an undergraduate, I studied operations research and financial engineering, and then I decided to get a PhD in computer science and business.
turns.zh: 我这条路走得挺绕的，所以我不确定自己是不是一个'标准范例'。不过我最初其实是以工程师身份出发的。本科我学的是运筹学（operations research）和金融工程（financial engineering），后来决定去拿一个计算机+商学方向的 PhD。

turns.en: Again, an engineering school that was granting the degree, and studying change was nowhere near my mind. And I had to take a graduate sequence in microeconomics to get my degree, and while I was in that class, I had sort of a revelation.
turns.zh: 而且学位还是工程学院颁的，'研究改变'这件事当时完全不在我脑子里。为了毕业我被迫修一门研究生级别的微观经济学课，就在那门课上，我忽然有种被点醒的感觉。

turns.en: The course was introducing all your classic economic concepts, but then it also blended in some of the new theories that were coming out of this new growing field of behavioral economics, which acknowledged that people are imperfect decision makers that were impulsive and overweight present utility or present value and underweight the long-term rewards of our actions, for instance.
turns.zh: 课上会讲那些经典经济学概念，但也掺进了一些正在兴起的行为经济学（behavioral economics）里的新理论——它承认人是不完美的决策者：容易冲动，会高估当下的效用或现值（present value）、低估我们行为的长期回报。

turns.en: And so all of these problems that are systematic with the way we make decisions were part of the class, and it just clicked for me. I loved it.
turns.zh: 所有这些关于'人做决策时系统性的偏差'的东西都是课上的内容——一下就击中了我。我彻底爱上了。

turns.en: I thought, oh my gosh, this is a perfect description of me, my life, everyone I know. It's fascinating. And once I understood that there were these mistakes people made, I started seeing opportunities in my own life to try to correct them.
turns.zh: 我心想：天哪，这不就是在说我自己、我的生活、我认识的每一个人吗？太迷人了。一旦理解了人有这些系统性的错，我就开始在自己的生活里找机会去修正它们。

turns.en: I started actually doing work on change initially just as a program of research rather than research. Why can't I get myself to go to the gym?
turns.zh: 我最初研究'改变'其实更像是给自己设的一个生活项目（program of life），还不算真正的研究——比如，我怎么就没法逼自己去健身房？

turns.en: Why can't I get myself to do my problem sets at the end of a long day? Oh, here's an idea, and then it would grow into a research project. So I pivoted, and then it really all clicked for me.
turns.zh: 为什么忙完一整天我还是逼不动自己做习题？然后突然冒出一个点子，点子又长成了一项研究课题。于是我就转型了，从此一切都通了。

turns.en: Actually, when I was an assistant professor at Wharton, I'd been doing research on behavioral science. A little bit of it was this change-oriented work due to my research interests, but it was all over the place.
turns.zh: 其实我在沃顿（Wharton）当助理教授的时候，就已经在做行为科学方面的研究。因为兴趣，也做了一点偏'改变'的工作，但当时很散。

turns.en: And I went to a seminar presentation over at the medical school at the University of Pennsylvania, and I saw this graph. There probably aren't that many people who can say their lives were changed by a graph, but my life was changed by a graph.
turns.zh: 有一次我去宾夕法尼亚大学医学院听一个学术报告，看到了一张图。能说自己人生被一张图改变的人应该不多，但我就是其中之一。

turns.en: And it was a graph showing the percentage of premature deaths in the US that are due to different causes. And the largest wedge in that graph was 40% due to behaviors that we could change.
turns.zh: 那张图显示的是：美国过早死亡（premature death）中，归因于不同原因的百分比。图里最大的一块——40%——归因于那些我们可以改变的行为。

turns.en: So decisions about things like eating, drinking, smoking, vehicle safety. I just couldn't believe how large the effects were of those small decisions.
turns.zh: 也就是关于吃、喝、抽烟、行车安全这些决策。我简直不敢相信这些小小的决策，累积起来影响可以这么大。

turns.en: The way that they accumulated was it was vastly larger than I would have expected, an order of magnitude. And that moment really changed my focus.
turns.zh: 它们的累积效应远超我原来的预期，大了整整一个数量级。那一刻真正把我的研究重心扭过来了。

turns.en: I realized, OK, this stuff that I've been doing sort of as a hobby for fun, this research on behavior change. If I really focus on this, there's a huge opportunity here to have a big social impact, because if we can figure out what it takes to help people make better decisions around their health, and then, of course, you can extrapolate to other domains like their financial decisions and their decisions about their education and happiness,
turns.zh: 我意识到：我一直在当爱好玩的这套东西——行为改变的研究——如果我真正聚焦上去，其实蕴含着一个巨大的社会影响力机会。因为如果我们能搞清楚怎么帮人们在健康上做出更好的决策，那自然可以外推到金融决策、教育决策、幸福决策——

turns.en: the accumulation is clearly much larger than I appreciated. So that's when I became really focused on behavior change, and that's what I've been really studying ever since.
turns.zh: 累积效应远比我原先估的要大得多。从那时起我就真正聚焦到行为改变上，一直研究到现在。

turns.en: What was the first insight you got before you started diving in from your MeSearch? I love that term. The first insight from my MeSearch had to do with the struggle I had as a graduate student.
turns.zh: 在你正式投入之前，你的 MeSearch（'自我研究'）给你的第一个洞见是什么？我特别喜欢这个词。——我 MeSearch 的第一个洞见，跟我读研时那种挣扎有关。

turns.en: When I was in an intense engineering program, I had to take economics classes and computer science classes and all these problem sets, and I would come home exhausted from listening to the lectures that I had to attend.
turns.zh: 当时我那个工程项目强度很大，我要上经济课、计算机课，做一堆习题。光是硬撑着听完那些课回家，人就累瘫了。

turns.en: I needed to get to my work, I needed to do my problem sets and write code, but I also needed exercise, because that was the only thing, frankly, that kept me sane was to be in good shape and moving, and I couldn't motivate myself to do either.
turns.zh: 我有一堆活儿要赶——习题要写、代码要写；但同时我也需要运动。坦白讲，那是唯一让我保持理智的东西——保持身体状态、动一动。可这两件事我都逼不动自己。

turns.en: I'd come home and all I wanted to do was curl up on the couch with a juicy page-turner or binge-watch TV, and I couldn't figure out, how do I resolve this problem?
turns.zh: 回到家我只想蜷在沙发上，看一本让人停不下来的小说，或者刷剧。我完全不知道这个问题该怎么解。

turns.en: I'm not getting any of the things done I needed to get done, and I came up with a solution. I call it now temptation bundling, and I've studied it in MeSearch research, and the idea was I just only allowed myself to enjoy those temptations, those entertainment temptations when I was exercising at the gym.
turns.zh: 我该做的事一件都做不完。后来我想到一个办法，现在叫'诱惑捆绑'（temptation bundling），我把它做成了 MeSearch 里的研究。思路就是：我只有在健身房边锻炼的时候，才可以享受那些诱惑、那些娱乐。

turns.en: I actually did it with audiobooks because I found the sensory input from TV was a little too much for my puny little brain at the end of a long day, but I'd go to the gym, I'd listen to the latest in my James Patterson novel, or sometimes just Harry Potter, or Hunger Games, Twilight, pick your lowbrow fiction that's fast-paced. I couldn't wait to get there. I'd come home, rush to the gym to find out what happened next. The time would fly while I was at the gym. I
turns.zh: 我用的是有声书，因为忙完一天之后，电视的感官刺激对我这个'小脑袋瓜'有点太猛。所以我去健身房，听 James Patterson 小说的最新一章；有时候就是《Harry Potter》、《饥饿游戏》、《Twilight》——你随便挑那种节奏飞快的通俗小说。我迫不及待。回到家直奔健身房，好知道下面剧情怎么样。在健身房那段时间'嗖'地就过去了。我

turns.en: didn't even notice it was passing, so I got a great workout in, and I came home, and I was ready to get my work done, and my grades improved, my happiness improved. It was fabulous, and I realized, okay, what had happened there was I had recognized the challenge of getting myself to do the things that were good for me in the long term required me to find a way to make them instantly gratifying, make them rewarding in the short term, or else I would never motivate myself to do it,
turns.zh: 都没察觉时间已经过去。所以我既锻炼了个好身体，回家又有精神干活，成绩提升了，幸福感也提升了。太爽了。我意识到——真正发生的是：我发现要逼自己做长期对自己有益的事，就得想办法让它'当下就有爽感'、短期里就有回报；不然我永远都逼不动自己去干，

turns.en: and so I recognized that barrier, I found an engineered solution, and for me it was a huge, huge gain. Temptation bundling, of course, I have since realized and recognized can help with lots of things, not just getting you to the gym, but you can use temptation bundling as a lure or a hook to get you to do things like studying by only allowing yourself to pick up your favorite coffee drink or other snack on your way to hit the books, or only letting yourself listen to your
turns.zh: 所以我识别到了障碍，找到了一个'工程化'的解法，对我自己收益巨大。当然，诱惑捆绑后来我意识到它能帮到很多事——不只是把你拽到健身房。你可以把它当成一个'饵'或者'钩子'，比如只有在去学习的路上才允许自己买那杯最爱的咖啡或小食；或者只有在做家事的时候才允许自己听你——

turns.en: favorite podcast while doing household chores, or cooking a fresh meal for your family. There's all different ways that I've found a temptation bundle that can make it exciting and fun in the moment to do the thing that's good for you in the long run. So all of this research turns to research and you've just come out with this wonderful book, How to Change. Why don't we frame this by having you kind of take me through the highlight outline of the book and then we can
turns.zh: 最喜欢的那一期播客；或者只有在为家人做一顿新鲜饭的时候才允许。我找到各种各样的诱惑捆绑，可以让'当下做长期对自己好的事'变得让人兴奋、有趣。所以所有这些'自我研究'最终都长成了真正的研究。你刚出了这本特别棒的《How to Change》。我们能不能这样来展开：你先带我过一遍这本书的重点大纲，然后我们再——

turns.en: dive in? Well, the book is organized around a key principle that I've come to believe is the most important insight from all of the research I've done on behavior change, and that is that in order to successfully achieve change, we first have to understand what is the specific obstacle that we're up against in a given situation. The situation I just described, where I was having trouble getting to the gym, my obstacle was impulsivity. It wasn't tempting to go to the gym,
turns.zh: 深入进去聊？好。这本书是围绕一个我认为最重要的原则来组织的，也是我所有行为改变研究里最大的一个洞见——要想真正改变，我们必须先搞清楚：在特定情境里，我们具体遇到的障碍是什么。刚才我说的那个情境，我老逼不去健身房，我的障碍就是'冲动性'（impulsivity）。去健身房一点都不诱人，

turns.en: it was tempting to sit on the couch. And so I didn't have the willpower to actually get myself off the couch and to the gym, and I needed to make it tempting to exercise. So that's one example of a barrier. It's really different if the barrier is, say, forgetting. You can't remember to take your medication, that's the reason you're not doing it, you need a totally different kind of solution. And I've seen that too often organizations and individuals that are trying to change don't
turns.zh: 坐在沙发上才诱人。所以我没那个意志力把自己从沙发上拽到健身房，我得让'运动'这件事变得诱人。这是一个障碍的例子。但如果障碍是'忘事'呢——比如你老忘了吃药，那你需要的就是完全不同的解法。但我看到太多想改变的组织和个人，并没有

turns.en: recognize the importance of figuring out what obstacle they're up against. They instead just look for sort of a shiny, nice sounding solution, a one size fits all, like let's set big audacious goals or visualize success and that'll get us there. But if you don't take account of what is actually blocking change, what are the barriers, you can't use the best scientific principles to solve the problem. So the book is organized around these different problems. So the first
turns.zh: 意识到'搞清楚对手到底是什么障碍'的重要性。他们更愿意去找那种听起来金光闪闪、放之四海而皆准的方案，比如'我们定一个宏大目标'、'我们想象成功'——然后就到位了。但如果你不去考虑到底什么东西在阻断改变、有哪些障碍，你就用不上最好的科学原理。所以这本书是按不同的问题来组织的。第一章

turns.en: chapter is about the getting started problem, which is just how do you get yourself over the hump from saying, yeah, someday I'd like to, to actually taking action or being ready to take action. I start with the getting started problem, then I pivot to impulsivity, which is essentially temptation, the challenge that we overweight things that are good for us in the short term and underweight the value we'll get in the long run. The next chapter is about procrastination,
turns.zh: 讲的是'启动问题'（getting started problem）——你如何从'嗯，我哪天要怎样'迈过那道坎，真正开始行动、或者准备好开始行动。我先讲启动问题，然后转到'冲动性'——本质上就是诱惑——我们总是高估短期对自己有利的东西、低估长期价值。下一章讲'拖延'（procrastination），

turns.en: which is very closely related to impulsivity. From there, I turn to the forgetting problem, which I could probably just as easily have termed flake out, what's salient, what comes to mind, whether or not we can keep it top of mind when it needs to be, which I actually think people under appreciate the importance of and can be really valuable to get that right.
turns.zh: 它跟冲动性联系非常紧密。接着讲'遗忘问题'（forgetting），我其实也可以叫它'掉链子'（flake out）——什么是显著的、什么会浮现在脑子里、我们能不能在该想起的时候把它保持在最显眼的位置。我觉得大家严重低估了这个东西的重要性，把它做对能带来很大价值。

turns.en: From there, I turn to the challenge of laziness, which I actually would argue is a good design feature for the human mind that we prefer the path of least resistance. We generally look for the easy way out. It makes a lot of sense. It's very efficient. And yet it creates challenges when we want to change. So laziness is a big one. From the laziness chapter, I turn to confidence, because another barrier to change is believing that we can. So figuring out how to make sure we
turns.zh: 接着讲'懒惰'这个挑战——我其实认为懒惰是大脑一个很好的设计：我们偏爱'阻力最小的路径'（path of least resistance），我们总想找一条轻松的路。这非常合理、非常高效，但当我们想要改变的时候就会制造麻烦。所以懒惰是个大问题。从懒惰这一章我转到'自信'——因为另一个改变的障碍，是'我们相不相信自己能行'。所以怎么确保我们

turns.en: have the confidence and the self-efficacy to put it in the term a psychologist would use al-Bendura's word, to actually pursue change is really important. And then from there, I turn to conformity. And this is where the social comes in. Who are your peers? Are they obstructing change?
turns.zh: 真正拥有追求改变的信心和'自我效能感'（self-efficacy，心理学家 Bandura 会用的词）非常重要。然后再转到'从众'（conformity）——这里'社会性'就出场了。你的同伴是谁？他们是在阻碍改变，

turns.en: Are they supporting change? Are they showing you the way? Are they showing you that it's impossible? So conformity is a really important barrier and sometimes solution to change.
turns.zh: 还是在支持改变？他们是在给你指路，还是在向你证明这事不可能？所以从众既是非常重要的改变障碍，有时候又是解决方案。

turns.en: And finally, the last chapter isn't really about a barrier so much as the important question of how do we keep at it? How do we maintain change and change in the long run?
turns.zh: 最后一章讲的不算是障碍，而是一个特别重要的问题——我们怎么坚持下去？怎么长期维持改变？

turns.en: There's a lot to unpack. And I think we should start at the top. And then maybe I'll just pick out a few. And particularly, we can keep going back and forth on this personal behavior change.
turns.zh: 内容量很大。我想我们从头开始吧，然后我挑几个重点。尤其可以在'个人行为改变'这块来回深入，

turns.en: And some of it relating to the financial markets investing. So getting started, obviously what comes to mind are New Year's resolutions or goal setting or whatever it is.
turns.zh: 一部分也关联到金融市场和投资。先说启动问题——大家脑子里第一反应的肯定是新年决心（New Year's resolutions）、目标设定之类。

turns.en: So what is it that helps people get started when they're trying to make change happen? Well, first, I love that you said what comes to mind as New Year's resolutions because that small insight that New Year's resolutions are sort of a special moment is actually what got me going on research on getting started. So I was giving a talk at Google about some of my work on how we could nudge people to make better financial decisions, better decisions about their health.
turns.zh: 那么在人想要推动改变的时候，什么能帮助他们启动？——首先，我特别喜欢你刚才说'脑子里第一反应是新年决心'，因为'新年决心是个特殊的时刻'这个小洞见，正是我研究启动问题的起点。我之前在 Google 做了一场演讲，讲的是怎么助推（nudge）人们做出更好的金融决策、更好的健康决策。

turns.en: And I got this question that was so, I thought, important and unstudied as far as I could tell, which was, okay, Katie, we're convinced that we should be using these tools and tactics to change our employees' behaviors. They'll be more productive and healthier and more excited. But is there some ideal time to provide them with these opportunities?
turns.zh: 结果有人问了一个我觉得非常重要、而且几乎没人研究过的问题——'Katy，我们已经被说服：应该用这些工具和策略来改变员工的行为，员工会更有生产力、更健康、更有干劲。但是——是不是有一个最理想的时点来给他们这些机会？

turns.en: Is there some ideal time to give them a nudge? And I have the same insight that you just mentioned. New Year's resolutions. I know New Year's is a thing. 40% of Americans make resolutions.
turns.zh: 是不是有一个最佳时点来给他们一记助推？'我脑海里浮现的也正是你刚才提到的那个——新年决心。我知道元旦是'大日子'，40% 的美国人会立新年决心。

turns.en: Something's going on there. There's something about that timing. But what it led me and my collaborators to realize when we started thinking carefully about this question and this problem is that New Year's is actually just one moment that has a feature that's really important and it's shared by all these other moments. And that feature is that it feels like a new beginning.
turns.zh: 这个时点肯定有什么玄机。当我们和合作者开始仔细琢磨这个问题时，我们意识到：元旦只是具备某个重要特征的时刻之一，而这特征是很多其他时刻也共享的——那个特征就是：它让人有一种'新的开始'（new beginning）的感觉。

turns.en: It essentially marks a chapter break in the way we think about time. And when we encounter a new beginning in life, we feel like whatever happened in the last chapter, well, that was the old me.
turns.zh: 它本质上是我们感知时间的方式里的一个'章节切换'（chapter break）。当生活里出现一个新的开始，我们会觉得：上一个章节里发生的一切——那都是'旧的我'。

turns.en: And this is the new me. And the new me doesn't have that baggage. The new me can do it. Last year, I didn't make good investment decisions. Or last year, I didn't quit smoking. Whatever the failings I had last year, I feel like that's old news and the new me can do it. And I'm also more likely to step back and think big picture about my goals at these moments that feel like chapter breaks in life. So what we've found in our research is that New Year's is just one example.
turns.zh: '现在是新的我，新的我没有那堆包袱，新的我可以做到。'去年投资没做好，去年没戒烟——whatever 去年我搞砸了什么，都是旧闻了，新的我可以做到。而且这些'章节切换感'的时刻，我也更愿意跳出来、从大局去想我的目标。所以我们研究里发现：元旦只是一个例子。

turns.en: There are lots of other dates ranging from the start of a new week or a new month to the celebration of a birthday or even a holiday that's associated with a fresh start can even be something like the start of spring. There are all of these moments that feel like chapter breaks. And of course, you can get to real chapter breaks that aren't just psychological and see even bigger effects like you move to a new home or you end up with a new job, you become a parent. Those
turns.zh: 还有很多其他日期——新的一周开始、新的一个月开始、生日、哪怕一个和'重新开始'关联的节日，甚至春天的开始——所有这些时刻都有'章节切换感'。当然，你也可以碰到真正不是心理层面、而是现实层面的章节切换，那种效果更大：搬新家、换新工作、成为父母。那些

turns.en: moments also demarcate time for us and change our motivation. So we've seen this both descriptively when we just analyze data, we see that people set goals more at these dates. They go to the gym more frequently around these fresh start dates. They're more likely to search the term diet on Google around these dates. And we can use it as a nudge or a lever when we encourage people, for instance, to start saving in a 401k plan who aren't yet saving. And we invite them to begin
turns.zh: 时刻也在为我们划定时间的分界、改变我们的动机。描述性上，我们从数据里就能看到：人在这些日期上会更多地设定目标；在这些'新起点'（fresh start）日期去健身房的频率更高；在 Google 上搜'diet'（节食）的概率更高。而且我们也能把它当成一个助推或杠杆。比如，鼓励那些还没开始往 401(k) 里存钱的人开始存——我们邀请他们在

turns.en: saving at a future date. If we say, do you want to start saving on your birthday or after your next birthday? That turns out to lead to about 30% more savings in the next eight months than inviting someone to start saving at an equal time delay. So if your birthday is in three months, we flip a coin randomly assign you to either get invited to save after your birthday or in three months. So identical offers, but one calls to mind this fresh start date. And that one that calls
turns.zh: 未来某个日期开始存。比如我们问：你想在生日那天、还是生日之后开始存？结果发现：未来 8 个月里存的钱，比'同样时间延迟后开始存'的对照组多约 30%。具体说，如果你生日在 3 个月后，我们就抛硬币随机分配你到'生日之后开始存'或'3 个月之后开始存'两组。两个 offer 是一模一样的，只不过一个想起了'新起点'日期。那个让人想到

turns.en: to mind the fresh start date leads to more savings. So these are all different ways that we've seen. We can use time and time markers to create a sense of a new beginning and motivate people to change at those moments. So on the other hand, as you think about this, let's say you have a good habit formation. You can imagine you're in a great workout regimen and then you go on vacation and it breaks it. How do you think about the other side of that of these periods of times
turns.zh: 新起点日期的那一组，存得更多。这些都是我们看到的方法：我们可以用时间、用时间标记，营造一种'新开始'的感觉，从而在这些时刻推动人改变。——反过来讲——假设你已经养成了一个好行为，比如你正在一个很好的健身节奏里，然后度个假就断了。这些'打断'的时候你怎么处理？这些打断期

turns.en: that come up that are disruptive and trying to maintain good habits on the other side of that? Yeah, I love that you asked that because there's this ugly underbelly of the fresh start effect, as we call it, which is that disruption is good when things are not going well. Disruption is good when you have a new goal you need to get motivated to start. But when things are going well, disruptions are harmful. And there's this wonderful study that my former student,
turns.zh: 里，怎么去维护好已有的好习惯？——我太喜欢你这个问题了。因为'新起点效应'（fresh start effect）有一个丑陋的'B 面'——当事情进展不顺时，'打断'是好事；当你有一个新目标需要被激起来启动时，'打断'也是好事。但当事情顺利推进时，'打断'是有害的。我以前的学生做了一项特别好的研究——

turns.en: Heng Chen Dai, who's now a UCLA professor did as her dissertation project. She and I had done this work I just described on the fresh start effect together. And she wanted to explore whether it might be a double-edged sword. We had an intuition and some early data suggesting that it might be harmful. And it made total sense, theoretically, but she wanted to collect real data on it. So she ran some experiments showing this, but my favorite study is one that she ran looking at
turns.zh: Hengchen Dai，现在 UCLA 的教授——这是她博士论文里的项目。她和我一起做过我刚才讲的那个新起点效应的研究。她想去探索这个效应是不是一把'双刃剑'。我们之前有种直觉，也有一些早期数据显示它可能是有害的。这在理论上完全讲得通，但她想真的收集数据来验证。所以她做了一些实验，我最喜欢的一个研究，是她去看了

turns.en: baseball players. She looked at baseball players who were either traded across leagues in the middle of the season or were traded within leagues in the middle of the season and compared what happened to those players, depending on whether they'd been performing really well earlier in the season or really poorly. And the reason she compared players who were traded across versus within leagues is one gets more of a fresh start than the other with that change. When you're traded
turns.zh: 棒球员。她看了赛季中被'跨联盟转会'的球员、以及赛季中被'联盟内转会'的球员，然后比较他们转会后的表现，取决于他们在赛季早期打得很好还是很差。她之所以对比'跨联盟转会'和'联盟内转会'，是因为前者带来更彻底的'新起点'。当你被转会到

turns.en: within league, your season-to-date statistics just keep on trucking. They keep on tracking. But if you're traded across leagues, you get a fresh start, a clean slate, they wipe that off, and you have to start from zero with your batting average and so on. So a bigger fresh start. And what she found is that for people who were traded across leagues and are getting this bigger fresh start compared to people traded within leagues, there was a bigger boost if you'd had a rough
turns.zh: 同一个联盟内的另一支队时，你整个赛季到目前为止的统计数据会一直累计。但如果你被跨联盟转会，你就获得了一个真正'干净的新起点'——那些数据被清掉，你打击率等等都从零开始。所以是更大的新起点。她发现：跨联盟转会、拿到更大新起点的那批人，相比联盟内转会的——如果你之前打得很烂，

turns.en: season in terms of performance. So you get a little benefit from the fresh start either way. It might just be regression to the mean, but where you can see something real is it's a bigger effect when you're traded across leagues with this fresh start. But the ugly part is, if you were doing really well, you're an above average performer and you get traded across leagues and have to start from scratch, now you get a bump down. So it's harmful because you lose that
turns.zh: 表现很糟糕——那么新起点带来的提升就更明显。无论哪种转会你都会得到一点点新起点的好处，那也许只是均值回归（regression to the mean）。但真正看得清楚的是：跨联盟转会、更大的新起点，那个效应更大。但丑陋的一面是——如果你本来打得非常好、高于均值，却被跨联盟转会、要从零开始，那就会往下掉。所以它是有害的，因为你丢掉了

turns.en: traction, you lose that momentum. And so there's other ways that this has been looked at as well, but I just love that illustration. And it does highlight that we have to be really conscious when things are going well of what may disrupt us, whether it's a vacation, a reset in the way our performance is being tracked at work because we have monthly sales records, for instance, whatever it is that could disrupt our flow and our success, that can be harmful. And if we can
turns.zh: 之前的'推动力'，丢掉了势头。别人也用其他角度研究过这个，但我特别爱这个例子。它提醒我们：当事情进展顺利的时候，我们得格外留意那些可能打断我们的东西——无论是休假、还是工作里'绩效统计方式的重置'（比如按月统计的销售数据），任何可能打断我们的'节奏'和'成功'的东西，都可能有害。如果我们能

turns.en: plan for it and try to figure out how to avoid the disruption, that may be beneficial. So I love the way you frame this book. I had James Clear on earlier in the year, a couple of years after Atomic Cavits came out. And a lot of his prescription was, okay, thanks, Katie Lake. We now know when to start. And he said, okay, we're going to make it easy, we're going to do these couple of things. You walk through the other side, which as you mentioned,
turns.zh: 提前规划、想办法避开这些打断，那可能是有益的。——我特别喜欢你给这本书搭的框架。James Clear 早一点（《Atomic Habits》出版后几年）来过节目。他给出的建议大多是'好，现在我们知道什么时候启动了'，他说'那我们要把事变容易，做这几件具体的事'。而你走的是另一面——就是你刚才讲的

turns.en: all these obstacles and how to get past the obstacles. And I'd love to just pick apart a few of them. And I want to start with confidence. So why don't you first describe, you did a little bit earlier, but what is it that is the obstacle that confidence creates in trying to make change happen? Yeah, it's funny. And I have to say, by the way, that it was a little bizarre as a behavioral scientist to write a chapter about boosting confidence, because we spend a lot of our time,
turns.zh: 所有这些障碍、怎么跨过障碍。我特别想挑几个来拆开聊。我想先从‘自信’开始。你能不能再详细讲讲，虽然刚才稍微说了一点——‘自信’这件事在推动改变时是怎么变成障碍的？挺好笑的。顺便说一句，作为一个行为科学家，写一章‘如何提升自信’其实挺怪的。因为我们花很多时间在——

turns.en: one of the things I teach all my Wharton students is we're all overconfident, we all think we're above average, and it's really harmful. And so it is peculiar to be focused on it. But of course, while it's harmful to be overconfident in many contexts, if you're trying to pursue goals, and you don't believe you can, you don't get as far. And in fact, overconfidence, while I would never prescribe it, but it does have some advantages for goal pursuit. And you can see why it might
turns.zh: 我教所有沃顿学生的一个观点就是：我们都过度自信（overconfident），都觉得自己高于平均水平——这是非常有害的。所以聚焦'提升自信'确实有点奇怪。但当然，虽然很多情境下过度自信有害，如果你在追求目标的时候都不相信自己能做到，你就走不远。事实上，过度自信——虽然我不会开这个方子——但在追求目标上确实有一些优势。所以你也能理解，为什么它

turns.en: even be that we ended up with that treat in the first place that that it might get you up in the morning. So it was funny to write this chapter. And it was funny, actually, the first piece of email I got complaining about my book was from a scientist friend who studies overconfidence who was like, Are you sure you should have had a chapter that was telling people to be more overconfident?
turns.zh: 甚至人类一开始就是进化出了这种'甜头'——它也许能让你早上愿意爬起来。所以写这一章挺有意思。有意思的是，我收到的第一封抱怨这本书的邮件，来自一位研究过度自信的科学家朋友，他说：'你确定要在书里有一章是让大家更过度自信吗？'

turns.en: And he was right. I tried to walk the line and said, Yes, I agree, people are generally overconfident, that's bad. However, this book is about what are the things we can do when we see a berry? And one berry is sometimes people just don't believe they have what it takes. And so they won't put in the effort. They won't lean in. And I have to note, I just said lean in, I wasn't really meaning to harkish that. But maybe it was subconscious. It is the case that women and minorities,
turns.zh: 他是对的。我尽量走中间线——我承认人普遍过度自信，这不好。但这本书讲的是：当我们看到'障碍'的时候我们能做点什么？其中一个障碍就是——人有时候根本不相信自己有那个能力，于是他们不下功夫、不向前倾。我得说一句：我刚才说'lean in'（向前倾/主动投入），我本来不是要去致敬那本书，但也许潜意识里有。确实，女性和少数群体，

turns.en: the circumstances they face, confidence tends to be a bigger issue for those subpopulations. And so I think it was particularly important to me, I've sometimes studied bias. When I'm not studying behavior change, it was important to me to have something in the book that I also felt would particularly benefit those groups. So what are the mechanisms that you'd want to put in place? You could take that as an example of, say, people are interested in making sure they
turns.zh: 由于他们所处的环境，自信对这些人群往往更是个问题。所以对我来说这一点尤其重要。我有时候也研究偏见（bias）——不研究行为改变的时候——所以我很想在书里也放一些内容，专门对那部分人群有帮助。那么——具体应该设立什么机制？我们可以拿一个例子：比如，一家机构想让

turns.en: have a more diverse workforce. How do you go about getting past that confidence obstacle? Well, there's really different answers for the organization that wants to hire a more diverse workforce. And for the individual who is trying to pursue their own goals and is facing a world where they are hearing negative stereotypes and need to step up to the plate in spite of all the negative feedback that they might get. I'll tell you one study. We found that if you hire in
turns.zh: 员工队伍更多元。怎么跨过'自信'这个障碍？其实答案要分两种——一种是'想招更多元员工的组织'该怎么应对；另一种是'个体在自己追求目标，但周围世界不断给他负面刻板印象，他还得硬着头皮上场'。我讲一个研究。我们发现：如果你是'批量招人'——

turns.en: sets, like you hire five people at a time instead of one person at a time, people choose to hire more diverse groups because diversity is not a property of an individual, but it is of a group.
turns.zh: 比如一次招 5 个而不是一个一个招——人们就会招到更多元的组合。因为'多样性'（diversity）是群体的属性，不是个体的属性。

turns.en: And if you value diversity, even if you're trying hard to take it into account and you want to work towards a more diverse goal, when you're hiring singletons one at a time, you may one at a time hire people who all look the same. When you hire five people, it jumps out at you that, wow, they all look the same. This is not okay. And so you're more likely to hire diverse groups when you hire in sets than in singletons. When I focus on the barrier of self-efficacy or self-confidence,
turns.zh: 如果你看重多样性，即便你一直在努力把它纳入考虑、一直奔着'更多元'的目标去——但当你一个一个地招时，你可能招进来的人都'长得一样'。一次性招 5 个，你立刻就意识到：哇，这些人看起来一模一样，这不行。所以批量招聘更容易招出多样性，一次一个则不然。当我们聚焦'自我效能感/自信'这个障碍时，

turns.en: it's more thinking about how can we equip the individual who wants to achieve more and has been facing feedback that makes them underconfident or a world that makes them underconfident, what can be done to address that specific issue.
turns.zh: 我们更多是在想：怎么给'想达成更多、但一直被让人不自信的反馈或世界包围'的那个人装备上工具，针对这个具体问题可以做些什么。

turns.en: So what can we do as individuals? So my favorite insight in the chapter comes from research that was done by Lauren Estrus-Winkler, who's about to be a new professor at the Kellogg School of Management at Northwestern. And she had this really brilliant insight when she was studying people and trying to figure out what separated high achievers from low achievers and doing all these interviews. And what she was really startled to discover was that even low achievers had a lot
turns.zh: 那么作为个体我们能做什么？这一章里我最喜欢的一个洞见来自 Lauren Eskreis-Winkler 的研究——她即将成为 Northwestern Kellogg 商学院的新教授。她在研究'人和人之间成就差距'、做大量访谈时，发现了一个特别漂亮的洞见。她震惊地发现：即便是'低成就者'，脑子里也有大量

turns.en: of great insights about how to be more successful. So salespeople who were struggling, students who were struggling, they weren't quite as clueless as she had envisioned. And she felt that one of the big barriers, though, was they lacked confidence in their abilities. And this seemed like it was a big blockade. She noticed that over and over again, they were being given advice. When someone heard that they were struggling, someone sort of put their arm around them and give them a bunch of
turns.zh: 关于'怎么更成功'的洞见。挣扎中的销售、挣扎中的学生，其实并不像她原先想象的那样一头雾水。她感到，其中一个大障碍是——他们不相信自己。这个信念缺失成了一个大闸门。她注意到，这些人反复被人'喂建议'——每当别人听说他们很挣扎，就会搂着他们的肩膀给一堆

turns.en: advice. Here's my tips on how to get better. That was actually really quite discouraging to have everyone you meet doling out their two cents as if you had no insight into your own condition and how to get better. And she wondered, what if we flip the script? If confidence is actually part of the problem, what if instead of putting our arm around someone's shoulder and coaching them, we actually asked them to coach someone else? What if we asked people who weren't achieving as
turns.zh: 建议。'我教你几个变好的方法。'其实这种'遇到谁都在给你支招、好像你对自己的处境完全没洞察'的场景，是非常让人泄气的。她就想：我们能不能把剧本翻过来？如果'自信不足'本身就是问题的一部分——与其搂着别人的肩膀教他们，不如请他们去教别人。如果我们去请那些'成就还没达到理想'的人

turns.en: much as they'd like to for advice on how to get better on achieving their own goal and to give it to someone else? And she thought a few things might happen here. One is it might boost your confidence. That was sort of the biggest thing, right? It puts you on a pedestal. You're a role model now. I'm telling you, I believe in you. You're so great that I want you coaching someone else.
turns.zh: 来给'如何达成自己的目标'提一些建议、并且拿去教别人呢？她认为这会引发几件事。第一：它能提升你的自信——这大概是最重要的。因为这等于把你放上'高台'，你现在是榜样。我在告诉你：我相信你，你太棒了，我想让你去指导别人。

turns.en: But she thought that would work in coordination with a couple other things. One is it might lead people to introspect a bit more about what could work for them as they're trying to dredge up insights about what advice to offer. And then it would feel hypocritical to coach someone to behave in a certain way and not behave that way yourself. So she's run a number of random assignment trials, and one of them we ran together looking at this. My favorite one was a study with high school
turns.zh: 她还觉得这会跟其他几件事联动。第一，这会让人更内省——在挖自己'该给别人什么建议'的时候，他们也在想什么对自己有效。第二，如果让别人按某种方式做、自己却不那么做，会觉得虚伪。所以她做了很多随机分配实验，其中一个我们也一起跑了。我最喜欢的一个是在高中学生里做的——

turns.en: students, about 2,000 of them, where we randomly assigned half of the students to give advice to their peers at the beginning of the second semester on how to be more effective in their study strategies.
turns.zh: 大约 2,000 人，我们随机分一半学生，让他们在第二学期开头给同学提供建议——怎么让学习策略更有效。

turns.en: We said, we want you to give some coaching to younger peers who are below you in school. How do you think they can study more effectively? And they spent about 10 minutes answering questionnaires to give advice. And then we had a control group that didn't go through this exercise. And we looked at the students' grades at the end of the third quarter, and we found that the students had significantly improved their grades who had been prompted to
turns.zh: 我们说：请你去给比你低年级的学弟学妹做一些指导，你觉得他们可以怎么更有效地学习？他们花大约 10 分钟填了一份'给建议'的问卷。另一边是不做这个练习的对照组。到第三季度末我们看学生的成绩，发现被邀请'给别人提建议'的那批学生，成绩显著提升

turns.en: give advice. In two areas, math, which was one of the areas we originally said we'd look at, and also in the class they told us they most wanted to improve in. And we didn't turn C students into valedictorians, but what we'd done was move them up about one point on a 50 to 100 scale, and it was significant, with 10 minutes of just asking them to be a mentor or a coach.
turns.zh: 在两块：数学——这是我们原本就打算看的一项，还有他们告诉我们'最想提高'的那门课。我们没把 C 学生变成毕业代表，但我们在 50 到 100 分制的量表上让他们平均往上大约 1 分——效果是显著的，只花了 10 分钟让他们去当一次'导师'。

turns.en: So I think the insight at the heart of this is when we give advice to others, when we are put in the position of mentors, it has all sorts of benefits, including boosting our confidence.
turns.zh: 所以我认为这件事的核心洞见就是：当我们给别人建议、当我们被放到'导师'这个位置上时，会带来各种各样的好处，其中包括提升我们自己的自信。

turns.en: And this is, I think there's a reason that programs like Alcoholics Anonymous not only give you a sponsor, but turn you into a sponsor when trying to help you stay sober, because by being in that role model mode, you actually benefit immensely. That's just one insight. There are others, but I think that's my favorite.
turns.zh: 我想，像戒酒互助会（Alcoholics Anonymous）这类项目，不光给你一位 sponsor，还会把你培养成一位 sponsor——是有道理的，因为进入'榜样模式'后你自己会获得巨大收益。这只是一个洞见，还有很多其他的，但我最喜欢这一个。

turns.en: Let's turn to conformity, which is sort of another interesting way of thinking about an obstacle in behavior change. Conformity is so interesting. And one of my favorite studies that illustrates this, which I talk about in the book, was done by UCSD economist Scott Carell. And he was interested in what the effect is of the roommate you're randomly assigned to live with your freshman year in college. And he actually got data from
turns.zh: 转到'从众'——它是理解行为改变障碍的另一个有意思的角度。从众特别有意思。我在书里讲过一个我特别喜欢的研究，是 UCSD 经济学家 Scott Carrell 做的——他研究的是：大学大一那年被随机分配到的室友，对你的影响有多大。他甚至拿到了

turns.en: his alma mater, the Air Force Academy, to see whether or not the roommate you're randomly assigned changes your grades. And he found that your roommate assignment does matter for your own performance, that being assigned a roommate who did better on the verbal SATs lifts you up and assigned to a roommate who did worse pushes you down. So that advice you got from your parents growing up to hang out with the right crowd, it does matter. The people were
turns.zh: 他母校——空军学院（Air Force Academy）——的数据，来看随机分配的室友会不会改变你的成绩。他发现室友分配确实重要：被分到 SAT 语文（verbal SATs）更高分的室友会把你抬起来，分到更低的室友会把你拖下去。所以你小时候父母说的'要跟对的人玩'，确实是有道理的。我们身边的人

turns.en: surrounded by influence all sorts of our decisions. By the way, they influence our interest in saving for retirement. They influence our interest in becoming an athlete or not. So they change us in all sorts of ways. One of the most potent ways is by showing us what's possible and giving us a sense of what we're capable of. So when we see other people who resemble us achieving more, we think, oh, that's doable. And also we may pick up insights about actually how to achieve. So
turns.zh: 会影响我们各种各样的决策。顺带说，他们也影响我们是否愿意为退休存钱、是否愿意成为运动员。他们以各种方式在改变我们。其中最有威力的一种，是'向我们展示什么是可能的、让我们重新感觉到自己的能力'。所以当我们看到和自己很像的人达成了更多，我们会想：'哦，这是可行的。'同时我们也可能拾到一些'到底怎么做到'的洞察。

turns.en: watching this roommate you ended up with who was so talented, hit the books and see, oh, they don't go out to parties on Wednesday nights. And that seems to turn out well for them. It can be that you realize, oh, I can emulate that. One of the things that I've studied that I find really interesting though is that people don't always pick up as much as they could from the people who surround them to get better at doing whatever it is they want to do. So we did this study where we
turns.zh: 比如你看到你的室友——那么有天分、那么用功——然后发现：哦，他周三晚上不出去派对，结果对他很好。于是你意识到：这个我可以模仿。但我自己研究里我觉得特别有意思的一点是——人们从周围的人身上'学到'的，往往不如他们本来能学到的那么多，本来可以帮他们把手上想做的事做得更好。所以我们做了一个研究，我们

turns.en: encouraged some people to deliberately copy and paste a strategy that was working for someone who had a similar goal. And that actually improved outcomes for these people. So it suggests that while we just naturally maybe through osmosis or observation, we see plenty of things rubbing off from the people around us, there's an opportunity to do even more and use conformity actually to be an asset by being really conscious of who are the people in my social network who are achieving
turns.zh: 鼓励一些人刻意去'复制粘贴'一个正在别人身上起作用、且目标相似者的策略。结果这些人的产出确实变好了。这说明：虽然我们天然地会通过耳濡目染、观察学到很多身边人的东西，但我们还能做得更多——把'从众'变成一项资产：真正有意识地去想——我的社交网络里，哪些人正在这个层次上达成目标——

turns.en: at this level and what are they doing and let me do it too. We're going to take a quick break in the action to tell you about Brookfield. Brookfield invests in the thing behind the thing behind the next big thing. Their focus across infrastructure, energy, real estate, private equity and credit is helping to build the backbone of the global economy. Brookfield combines deep operational expertise with disciplined long-term investing, uncovering value and partnering alongside
turns.zh: 他们在做什么？我也可以跟着做。——我们插播一段广告，讲讲 Brookfield。Brookfield 投的是'下一个大事件背后的背后的东西'。他们在基础设施（infrastructure）、能源、房地产、私募股权（private equity）、信用（credit）等领域的布局，正在帮助构建全球经济的骨架。Brookfield 把深厚的运营专业能力和长期纪律性投资结合起来，挖掘价值、与客户并肩

turns.en: clients to shape tomorrow's economy today. Invest in the businesses that shape tomorrow. Learn how you can own what's next at Brookfield.com slash own. This is not an offer to sell or investment advice. Investing involves risk, including the loss of capital. And now, back to the show.
turns.zh: 一起塑造未来的经济。投那些塑造明天的企业。想了解如何'拥有下一个'，请到 Brookfield.com/own。这不构成销售要约或投资建议，投资有风险，包括可能损失本金。好，我们回到节目。

turns.en: I'm really curious how this plays out in settings where they're either zero-sum games or it's not just a positive for everyone. So study habits, everybody could have better grades, but in investing, you could think if someone has a novel strategy and other people start copying it, it may not last. How do you think about where conformity in those situations is beneficial and where it might not be? Such a great question. It's so interesting. It certainly seems like in
turns.zh: 我很好奇，如果换到'零和游戏'（zero-sum game）或者'不是所有人受益'的场景，这套逻辑会怎么展开。比如学习习惯这件事，所有人都可以考更好；但投资里——如果一个人搞出了一种新颖策略，别人开始模仿，它可能就不会持续。你怎么判断在这些情境里'从众'什么时候有益、什么时候无益？

turns.en: that context, you're going to get benefits if you're a fast mover on conformity. If you follow the herd quickly enough, but you're right that if you wait too long and you conform slowly, then there's likely to be little benefit left. And perhaps you'll even get stuck holding the stock that was a bubble. And you bought it at the high. Oops. I'm just thinking about game stuff. So it's a challenge for sure. And I think this is a really interesting thing about
turns.zh: 这个问题太好了。太有意思了。那种场景下显然——

turns.en: conformity is that just like fresh starts, there's pros and cons. It's like a double-edged sword. And that's really the way I write about it in the book, as it can be an asset if you harness it correctly, but it also can be a barrier. It's hard to know what to say in terms of how do you detect when it will be one or the other? Like how do you know? And it probably, I feel like if I were a mathematician, right now I would try to write a model of what fraction of
turns.zh: 如果你是'快从众'的人，你确实能吃到从众的红利。跟得上羊群就跟得到；但你说得对——如果你等太久、从众太慢，剩下的好处可能就没了。搞不好你还被套在一只泡沫股上、买在了高点，糟糕。我脑子里在过博弈（game theory）这件事。这确实是个挑战。我觉得从众这件事很有意思的一点是——

turns.en: other people need to have already taken this action before it ceases to be advisable for you to follow. And you could sort of imagine trying to figure out the moment when it tips and you wouldn't want to be conforming because now in a zero-sum game you're actually losing out. But I guess like short of having a precise answer, I think the best answer is the faster you jump on the bandwagon, the better. And if you feel that you're late, maybe it's not actually going to be useful to do
turns.zh: 它跟'新起点'一样，是有利有弊的双刃剑。我在书里就是这么写的——用对了它是资产，用错了它是障碍。至于怎么提前分辨它是哪一种，我很难说清楚——你怎么能知道？如果我是个数学家，我大概现在会想去建一个模型——到底多少人已经采取了动作之后，

turns.en: it at all in a zero-sum context. So I guess that leads us right into procrastination. So even in that situation when we know that's the outcome, what are the things that prevent us from jumping on that bandwagon early? Yeah, procrastination is such an interesting barrier to change and it relates closely to impulsivity. It's sort of like what happens due to impulsivity is that we put things off that we should be doing because I can always get to it tomorrow,
turns.zh: 你再跟就不划算了——这个比例到底是多少。你可以想象有一个'翻转时刻'，一旦过了那个点，在零和游戏里你从众就是在赔钱。不过在没有一个精确答案之前，我觉得最好的答案是：跳上马车（bandwagon）越快越好。如果你感觉自己已经晚了，那在这种零和场景里，从众也许根本就没用。

turns.en: but today I have something that's more instantly gratifying. What I think is really interesting about procrastination is that the best solution seems to be a solution that we're really used to having other people impose on us but uncomfortable imposing on ourselves. So let me explain what I mean by that. It's common for the world or I'll say policymakers, teachers, parents to set up rules and regulations and systems that help us avoid procrastinating or
turns.zh: ——所以这就把我们带到'拖延'（procrastination）。既然我们知道那是结果，为什么我们还不能早点跳上车？——拖延是非常有意思的改变障碍，跟冲动性密切相关。因冲动性产生的问题，就是我们把该做的事往后推——'明天再弄也来得及'——

turns.en: making impulsive decisions. So things like deadlines in school for your assignments instead of everything you have to do for a class all being due at the end of the semester at the same time, help us not procrastinate and we're very used to that. Speed limits help us make the right choice in a situation where our impulses would lead us astray. We're used to being fined for bad behavior or having rules imposed on us by other people, but we're not so used to imposing them on ourselves
turns.zh: 但今天要享受一个当下更爽的事。拖延这件事特别有意思的一点是：最好的解决方案恰恰是我们非常习惯别人'给我们上'、但不太习惯'自己给自己上'的东西。让我解释一下。这个世界——政策制定者、老师、家长——常常在给我们设定各种规则、制度，帮我们避免拖延、

turns.en: and the best scientifically proven solution I've seen for procrastination and for a lot of willpower problems is actually constraining ourselves using what economists call commitment devices or tools that prevent us from making decisions, from procrastinating, from making choices that will be bad in the long run and impose some sort of penalty on us in fact if we do. So my favorite example of this is a study of people who are customers at Green Bank which is a bank in the
turns.zh: 避免冲动决策。比如学校里给作业设 deadline，而不是把所有课的作业全堆到学期末一起交——这就是帮我们不拖延，我们非常习惯。限速（speed limits）也是——在冲动会带我们跑偏的地方，它逼我们做对的选择。我们习惯了'做错事要被罚款'、习惯'别人给我们上规则'，但不太习惯'自己给自己上规则'。

turns.en: Philippines and the challenge there was that lots of people had leaky savings. They wanted to save more but a festival, a birthday comes up and the money comes right back out and the experiment that I find so interesting about commitment devices, about procrastinating to actually build that nest egg said what if we basically make it impossible for you to take money out of your account? What if we offer you a locked account where you can put money in but you can't take money out until you've
turns.zh: 而我见过的、被科学验证过的、对抗拖延和很多意志力问题的最好方案，是'约束自己'——经济学家叫它'承诺装置'（commitment devices）——那些阻止我们做某些决定、阻止拖延、阻止做长期对自己不好的选择；一旦做了，还会对我们施以某种惩罚的工具。我最喜欢的一个例子是关于 Green Bank 客户的研究——一家位于——

turns.en: reached a predetermined savings goal or predetermined date and of course there was a lot of skepticism will anyone want such an account? So this experiment was run where half of the customers in the population were just offered a standard savings account with a standard interest rate and the other half were also offered that standard account or this commitment account which had exactly the same interest rate as the standard account but these restrictions on access to your funds.
turns.zh: 菲律宾的银行。那里的挑战是——很多人的存款是'漏水'的：他们想多存钱，但一有节日、一有生日，钱就又流出去了。这个关于承诺装置、关于'拖延到攒出小金库（nest egg）'的实验我觉得特别有意思，它是这么设计的：如果让你的账户'基本没法把钱取出来'，会怎样？——给你一个'锁定账户'，钱只能存进去，达不到预设的储蓄目标或预设的日期之前不能取出来——

turns.en: So an economist would say no one should want that it's a worse account but actually about 30% of people offered this account took it and if you look at the two groups the one that was offered the account and the one that wasn't regardless of whether people use the account they saved 80% more so those 30% who said yeah I'm going to put some money in the account they saved so much more than 100% if you look at 100% of the people there's an 80% increase in savings.
turns.zh: 会怎样？当然很多人怀疑：会有人要这样的账户吗？于是他们做了一个实验：一半客户只拿到一个标准利率的标准储蓄账户；另一半客户除了标准账户，还多一个'承诺账户'（commitment account）——利率完全一样，但对支取有限制。

turns.en: So this is a really powerful tool finding ways to bind our hands as the story of Ulysses in in the Odyssey right Odysseus or Ulysses whichever you prefer to call him the story of binding his hands to the mast is the original story of a commitment device to avoid the temptation of shipwreck on an island occupied by sirens who sing sweet songs to lure sailors closer by where they'll inevitably die amid the rocks. It's a really powerful solution but one that people
turns.zh: 经济学家会说：没人应该要这个东西，这是个更差的账户。但实际上，被提供承诺账户的客户里大约 30% 用了它。而且——对比'提供账户'和'不提供账户'两组——无论是否真的使用那个账户，前者整体多存了 80%。也就是说：那 30% 用承诺账户的人存得非常多——以至于如果把 100% 的人都算进去，总储蓄也增加了 80%。

turns.en: tend to underuse and underappreciate. So we have a great corollary that in our world with locked up funds you think about private equity funds and venture capital funds if the benefit is so large even though you're tying your own hands are there situations where people are willing to pay for that benefit you could imagine a situation where even though I could say well I'm restricting my options that should be worse for me to be in this locked account if I do it I'm going to have
